---
title: "Platforms"
description: >-
  Which file formats each system's preview shows, what macOS, Linux and Windows each need, and how to extend them with plugins.
lightbox: auto
---

zotLook carries no viewer. It drives the preview the system already has, which
is why what you see is exactly what your file manager shows — third-party
preview extensions included.

## What each system needs

::: {.panel-tabset}

### macOS

Nothing to install. Quick Look is part of the system, and zotLook drives the
same panel the Finder does.

Requires macOS 12 (Monterey) or later.

The plugin ships a small compiled helper for this, `qlpreview`, as a signed
universal binary — it is the only compiled piece in the package.

### Linux

**GNOME Sushi**, the preview that Files (Nautilus) opens on Space.

```sh
sudo apt install gnome-sushi        # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install sushi              # Fedora
```

It need not be running: zotLook reaches it over D-Bus, and D-Bus starts it on
demand. It works outside GNOME as long as the service is installed and a session
bus is running.

One habit of the desktop carries over: the moment the preview opens, GNOME
hands it the keyboard, exactly as when Files opens it. From then on the window
answers its own keys — **Space**, **Escape** or **q** close it — and zotLook's
shortcuts cannot reach the plugin until Zotero is focused again, where the same
press that opened a preview still toggles it. That is Sushi behaving as
designed, not a binding gone missing.

The arrow keys belong to that design too: Sushi keeps them and reports each
press to whatever opened it as selection movement — that is how Files walks
its list with the preview open. zotLook answers the same way, switchable in
its settings: an arrow inside the preview moves the selection in your item
list, and the preview follows the moment the keys come to rest. It follows
with the plain preview whatever was showing, since a contact sheet for every
row passed through would mean seconds of rendering apiece. Scrolling inside
the preview itself stays the wheel's job — the Page keys join in after a click
into the preview window, which is what hands its content the keyboard
focus.

KDE has no comparable system-wide preview service — Kiview is a Dolphin
extension without an external interface — so nothing is driven there.

### Windows

**[QuickLook](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook)**, the open-source preview
that brings the Space key to Explorer. It must be **running**; zotLook talks to
it over the named pipe it listens on.

Both builds work: the Microsoft Store package and the desktop installer answer
alike. Older accounts of this integration say the Store build is sandboxed away
from the pipe — measured today, it is not.

The preview opens without taking focus away from Zotero, so the keyboard keeps
working where you are — and zotLook asks Windows to keep it that way even when
the preview was started with the mouse, from the context menu, which is the one
case where QuickLook could otherwise take it. The shortcut that opened a preview
closes it again, and so does **Escape**. Click into the preview and QuickLook's
own keys apply instead, until you click back.

:::

## What works where

| | macOS | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preview attachments | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Preview notes | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| EPUB rendered by zotLook | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Contact sheet | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Clicking a page opens the reader | ✓ | — | ✓ |
| Contact sheet in a Zotero window | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

The one gap is Sushi. Its renderer really does follow links, and it cannot load
a `zotero:` URL — so the links are made inert there on purpose, because a click
that fails takes the whole preview down with it. The last row is the
one where everything works everywhere: the window is Zotero's own, and [the
sheet in it](window.qmd) behaves identically on the three systems — with the
clickable sheet on Linux too. Why Sushi cannot follow is explained in [The
contact sheet](dev/contact-sheet.qmd).

## Seen side by side

The same three keystrokes on each system, each driving the preview that system
already has. What differs is the panel around the page, not what zotLook does.

The highlights are Zotero's own. They live in its database rather than in the
file, so what is previewed is an exported copy with them drawn in.

### How large the windows are

Only the sheet's Zotero window can be given a size: it keeps what it was
dragged to, and the [window size setting](settings.qmd#the-contact-sheet)
shows and sets the value — the same on all three systems, since the window is
Zotero's own.

The system previews decide their own size, and none takes one from outside:

- **macOS** sizes the Quick Look panel to the content and the screen.
- **GNOME Sushi** sizes its window to the viewer at hand, remembers nothing
  between two calls, and its D-Bus interface has no notion of size. A window
  enlarged by hand holds only while it is open. For a large sheet on Linux,
  use the Zotero window.
- **QuickLook for Windows** opens HTML, and so the sheet, at 1280 × 720
  pixels, fixed in its viewer plugin. A window resized by hand is kept until
  QuickLook quits; there is no setting for it, and the named pipe zotLook
  drives it through knows only open, switch and close.

## Which formats appear where

That is the preview program's business, not zotLook's. The table describes each
one as it comes; every column can be [extended](#extending-the-preview).

| Format | macOS | Linux | Windows |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **PDF** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Images** (JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF, WebP) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Camera RAW** | ✓ | partly¹ | ✓ |
| **Video** (MP4, MOV) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Video** (MKV, AVI) | — | ✓² | ✓ |
| **Audio** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **HTML** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Text and source code** | ✓³ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Markdown** | — | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Office** (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) | ✓ | ✓⁴ | ✓⁵ |
| **Archives** (ZIP, RAR, 7z) | — | — | ✓ |
| **EPUB** | **zotLook** | **zotLook** | **zotLook** |

¹ through the system's image loaders (glycin, formerly GdkPixbuf) ·
² through whichever GStreamer codecs are installed ·
³ known extensions only; see QLStephen below ·
⁴ through LibreOffice, where it is installed ·
⁵ through the *OfficeViewer* plugin, with no Office installed

**EPUB is the exception everywhere:** none of the three renders an e-book, so
zotLook converts it itself — the one format zotLook does not simply hand over.
Everything else your preview program can show, zotLook can show.

## Extending the preview

Because zotLook drives the system's preview, anything you install there works
**in Zotero straight away**. A viewer for a format zotLook has never heard of
does not have to be built into zotLook.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### macOS

Quick Look takes extensions as *Quick Look generators*. The easiest route is
[Homebrew](https://brew.sh):

```sh
brew install --cask qlmarkdown        # Markdown
brew install --cask qlvideo           # MKV, AVI, FLV and other video formats
brew install --cask qlstephen         # text files with no known extension
brew install --cask betterzip         # archives
brew install --cask syntax-highlight  # source code, with highlighting
brew install --cask webpquicklook     # WebP
```

[sindresorhus/quick-look-plugins](https://github.com/sindresorhus/quick-look-plugins)
keeps a maintained list. It leans towards free software and leaves out several
that suit a research library particularly well:

| Extension | Formats | |
|---|---|---|
| [**Book Preview**](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/book-preview/id6744098874) | **EPUB, MOBI**, FB2, **DJVU**, CBR, CBZ — with a table of contents | €7.99 |
| [**Glance**](https://github.com/samuelmeuli/glance) | source code (JSON, Python, YAML …), Jupyter, Markdown, TAR/ZIP | free |
| [**iPreview**](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/ipreview-powerful-quick-look/id1519213509) | as Glance, plus RAR, 7Z, AsciiDoc, TSV as a table, 3D models | €7.99 |
| **DicomPreview** | DICOM — X-ray and MRI images | free |
| [**QuickFits**](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/quickfits/id1551075981) | FITS — astrophotography | free |
| [**Camera RawX**](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/camera-rawx/id6587554858) | compressed RAF (Fuji), NEF (Nikon), X3F (Sigma) | €12.99 |
| [**Apparency**](https://mothersruin.com/software/Apparency/) | what an application is made of | free |

::: {.callout-tip title="Book Preview and zotLook's EPUB preview"}
Both show EPUBs, and both with a table of contents — zotLook's own conversion
[carries one](features.qmd#what-it-previews). So the choice is one of taste:
zotLook sets the book in a book-width Palatino column and keeps the publisher's
stylesheets, Book Preview shows it in its own presentation.

To give Book Preview the right of way, switch the conversion off in
[Settings](settings.qmd) and the book goes to Quick Look untouched.

For **MOBI, DJVU and the comic formats** there is no choice: zotLook cannot
convert those and only ever hands them over, so the extension is the only route
to a preview at all.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="When two extensions claim the same format"}
macOS decides which one wins, and not always in your favour: a Markdown editor
with a rudimentary extension can take precedence over the careful QLMarkdown.

The remedy is **System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions**, the
*Extensions* section, then the i beside *Quick Look*. On macOS 26 (Tahoe),
switch the view from "By App" to "By Category" first. An extension can be
disabled there without deleting the app it came with.

It cannot be decided per file type. An all-rounder such as Glance or iPreview
can only be switched off entirely — which is why several specialised extensions
are easier to steer than one universal one.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Quarantine, after installing"}
Since macOS Catalina the system marks downloaded extensions as quarantined, and
Quick Look then **silently declines to load them** — there is simply still no
preview. Clear it once:

```sh
xattr -d -r com.apple.quarantine ~/Library/QuickLook
```

Then run `qlmanage -r`, or log out and back in.

Extensions that arrive as an application produce a different complaint — macOS
"could not verify it is free of malware". Allow it under **System Settings →
Privacy & Security → Security → Open Anyway**. App Store extensions are checked
by Apple and spare you both.
:::

Extensions live in `~/Library/QuickLook` (yours) or `/Library/QuickLook`
(everyone's). Newer ones arrive as an app carrying a *Quick Look extension*,
which you enable under **System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions**.

### Linux

Since version 51 Sushi has a **plugin interface**: a plugin is a JavaScript file
deriving from the `Renderer` class, looked for in

```
$HOME/.local/share/sushi/plugins-1     # yours
/usr/lib/sushi/plugins-1               # everyone's
```

Before version 51 the directory was `$HOME/.local/share/sushi/viewers`.

::: {.callout-note title="Unlike the other two"}
There is no stock of ready-made Sushi plugins to download. The interface exists
and is described in
[plugins/Plugins.md](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/sushi/-/blob/master/plugins/Plugins.md)
— but whoever uses it writes the plugin themselves.
:::

In practice Sushi is therefore extended **indirectly**, through the system
libraries its viewers draw on:

| Install this | and Sushi shows |
|---|---|
| GStreamer codecs (`gstreamer1.0-plugins-bad`, `-ugly`, `-libav`) | more video and audio formats |
| image loaders (`webp-pixbuf-loader`, glycin loaders) | WebP, AVIF, HEIF |
| LibreOffice | DOCX, XLSX, PPTX |

That is not a workaround but the design: for these formats Sushi carries no code
of its own and uses what the system can already do.

### Windows

QuickLook takes extensions as `.qlplugin` files, and installing one is the
simplest of the three:

1. Download the `.qlplugin` from the plugin's releases page.
2. Select it in Explorer and press **Space** — QuickLook previews it itself and
   offers **Install**.
3. Restart QuickLook.

The project keeps the list under
[Available Plugins](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook/wiki/Available-Plugins).
Useful for academic work, among others:

| Plugin | Formats |
|---|---|
| **OfficeViewer** | Word, Excel, PowerPoint — with no Office installed |
| **JupyterNotebookViewer** | `.ipynb` |
| **SqliteViewer** | SQLite databases |
| **ShapefileViewer** | ESRI shapefiles |
| **FitsViewer** | astrophotography (FITS) |
| **Hdf5Viewer** | HDF5 datasets |
| **CADImport** | `.dwg`, `.dxf`, `.plt`, `.cgm` |
| **ExifTool** | metadata for many formats |

:::
